source.note: Market gilt rates: the weighted average interest rate on conventional gilts, used as the marginal cost of additional borrowing (ADR-0005).

derivation.formula: the OBR's market gilt rate path, year by year
derivation.note: March used a flat 10-year yield; October's determinants table publishes the path, so the engine follows it.

sensitivities.title: Bank Rate and gilt yields, +1 percentage point (sustained)
sensitivities.description: The OBR estimates that a 1 percentage point increase in gilt yields on new debt and in Bank Rate expectations across the forecast would add £13 billion to the current budget deficit in 2029-30 and £16 billion in 2031-32, through debt interest alone.

adjusts.how: adds the slider value to the marginal rate on new borrowing

sensitivities.rampNote: The OBR states 2029-30 and 2031-32. 2030-31 is the midpoint; 2028-29 and 2027-28 step back by £1 billion a year as refinancing builds; 2026-27 is set at about two-thirds of 2027-28 because Bank Rate passes through to reserves remuneration at once while gilt refinancing is gradual. The years between the stated points are assumptions.

source.quote: A 1 percentage point increase in gilt yields on new debt issued and on Bank Rate expectations across the forecast period, directly via its effect on debt interest payments, is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £13 billion in 2029-30 and £16 billion in 2031-32.

secondarySource.quote: A 1 percentage point change in gilt yields and Bank Rate expectations across the forecast could lead to a medium-term change in borrowing of £16 billion.

sensitivities.title: Nominal GDP growth, +0.1 percentage point a year
sensitivities.description: The OBR estimates that a 0.1 percentage point change in nominal GDP growth in each year from 2027-28 changes the current budget deficit by £5 billion in 2029-30 and £9 billion in 2031-32. Higher growth lowers borrowing.

adjusts.how: compounds both GDP denominators by (1 + growth change) each year from the first forecast year, 2027-28

sensitivities.rampNote: The OBR states 2029-30 and 2031-32. The path is assumed to build linearly from 2027-28 because the effect scales with the cumulative level of GDP.

source.quote: A 0.1 percentage point reduction in nominal GDP growth from 2027-28 is estimated to increase the current budget deficit by £5 billion in 2029-30 and £9 billion in 2031-32.

sensitivities.title: RPI inflation, +1 percentage point (sustained)
sensitivities.description: The OBR estimates that a 1 percentage point rise in RPI and CPIH inflation in each year of the forecast adds £9 billion to the current budget deficit in 2029-30 and £11 billion in 2031-32, through accrued interest on index-linked gilts alone.
sensitivities.rampNote: The OBR states 2029-30 and 2031-32. A flat profile to 2029-30 is assumed because the RPI uplift on index-linked gilts accrues immediately; 2030-31 is the midpoint. The OBR gives no separate figure for a fall this time.

source.quote: A 1 percentage point rise in RPI and CPIH inflation in each year of the forecast period, via its effect on accrued interest on index-linked gilts alone, is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £9 billion in 2029-30 and £11 billion in 2031-32.

sensitivities.title: Effective tax rate, +1 percentage point
sensitivities.description: A 1 percentage point change in the effective tax rate from 2027-28 changes the current budget deficit by £35 billion in 2029-30 and £38 billion in 2031-32. Informational: used for the uncertainty display, not a slider.

source.quote: A 1 percentage point reduction in the effective tax rate from 2027-28 is expected to increase the current budget deficit by £35 billion in 2029-30 and £38 billion in 2031-32, assuming no wider macroeconomic impacts.
Historically, the average absolute five-year forecast difference for receipts as a share of GDP is 0.9 percentage points.

source.note: The margin against the current budget target in 2029-30, after the Budget's measures; £12.5 billion before them.

source.quote: the current forecast margin of a fall of 0.7 per cent of GDP
source.note: Table A.9's rounded shares give 83.8 to 83.1, also -0.7.

notes: The Budget's measures are in this baseline. The OBR assessed the fiscal rules formally at this Budget: the current budget is in surplus by £14.5 billion in 2029-30 (the Treasury rounds it to £15 billion), the margin against the fiscal mandate; it was £12.5 billion before the measures, which add £2.0 billion.

HM Treasury's Chart 1.6 walks the margin from March: £23.6 billion, less £12.0 billion from the underlying debt interest forecast, plus £0.9 billion from other underlying changes, £12.5 billion before measures, plus £2.0 billion from policy, £14.5 billion.
Welfare spending inside the cap is forecast at £207.0 billion in 2029-30 after the inflation and Scottish block grant adjustments, £2.8 billion above the cap and margin of £204.2 billion (Table 7.2).

Not on Table 6.1 but in the baseline (Table 3.1, note 1): the £5.5 billion resource DEL assumption for 2031-32 and the unfunded public service pensions valuation, which moves about £15 billion a year from RDEL to AME from 2027-28. The adjusted triple lock from April 2030 does not change state pension costs inside the forecast (paragraph 3.50).
